name: time-duration
algorithm: Make n durations (splitmix64, seed 1: each the next output as a signed 64-bit value, shifted right arithmetically by the next output modulo 64, so every magnitude occurs), then rounds times write each in Go's Duration.String form ("1h2m3.5s") and parse the text back; the checksum adds per duration and round the parsed nanoseconds with the sign bit cleared and the text's length, wrapping.

skip.c: C's std has no duration type or text form
skip.rust: Rust's std writes a Duration with Debug ("1.5s") and has no parser
skip.zig: Zig's std.fmt writes a duration (fmtDuration) but has no parser
skip.mk-wrap: the checksum already uses the wrapping operators; the task has no other arithmetic to wrap

no_counts: B24 does not apply: an idiomatic row compares libraries; the functions are tested against Go by the lane's Go tests (status/std-time2.md)
notes: Mk: Duration.Format through Arena.Fmt (an arena per round, freed at its end), then time.ParseDuration. Go: Duration.String (a 32-byte stack buffer, then one string allocation), then time.ParseDuration. Both write and read the same text (TestStdTime_DurationFormatAgainstGo, TestStdTime_DurationAgainstGo).
Checksums agree between Mk and Go at both sizes on the owner's machine (std-time2 session 2, 2026-11-13).
Not published: no number here is a measurement.
